a b s t r a c t
Rodents are important reservoir hosts of many tick-borne pathogens. Their importance in the circulation
of the emerging bacterial agent, Candidatus Neoehrlichia mikurensis and the intraerythrocytic protozoan
parasite, Babesia microti has been recently proposed. The aim of the present study was to identify the
presence and genetic diversity of Candidatus N. mikurensis and B. microti circulating in the natural foci
among rodents and two species of ixodid ticks (Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes trianguliceps). In 2011–2013,
rodents were captured at sampling sites in Eastern Slovakia. A total of 997 rodents (324 Apodemus agrarius,
350 Apodemus flavicollis, 271 Myodes glareolus, and 52 other rodent species), 788 feeding ticks from
rodents, and 1375 questing ticks were investigated for the presence of pathogens by molecular methods
followed by DNA sequencing. Candidatus N. mikurensis was detected in
of questing I. ricinus nymphs
and
of questing adult I. ricinus ticks, spleens of rodents
, as well as in feeding larval I. ricinus
and feeding larval I. trianguliceps ticks
. The 16S rRNA and gltA gene sequences of Candidatus
N. mikurensis obtained in this study confirmed a high degree of genetic identity of this bacterium in
Europe. DNA of B. microti was found in ear
and spleen biopsies of rodents
, in rodent foetus
and feeding larval
and nymphal (8.7%) I. ricinus, in questing nymphal I. ricinus
and
questing adult I. ricinus ticks
. None of the 112 I. trianguliceps ticks were infected. B. microti was
represented by two different genotypes:
of the positive samples belonged to the zoonotic type strain
from Jena (Germany). The results of this study underline the importance of rodents in the circulation of
both emerging pathogens in natural foci.

Introduction
In Europe, Candidatus N. mikurensis represents a newly
emerging tick-borne zoonotic bacterium from the family Anaplas-
mataceae (Kawahara et al., 2004). It is an obligate intracellular
Gram-negative organism, transmitted by Ixodes ticks in temper-
ate regions of the Northern hemisphere (Schouls et al., 1999;
Vichova et al., 2014; Derdakova et al., 2014). Recently, Burri et al.
(2014) confirmed the reservoir competence of rodents for this bac-
terium in xenodiagnostic experiments. Moreover, it was detected
in the blood and endothelial cells of rodent spleens and liv-
ers proving systemic infection (Jahfari et al., 2012; Burri et al.,
2014). Candidatus N. mikurensis could not be cultivated in vitro
so far, therefore, the status “Candidatus” is still preserved. Since
2007 in Europe, only eight human cases of disease were reported,
mainly from immunocompromised patients (Welc-Faleciak et al.,
Babesia spp. represent widespread protozoan hemoparasites
from the family Babesiidae. Ixodes ricinus plays an important role
in the transmission of several protozoan species of the genus
Babesia. Babesia divergens, Babesia venatorum, and Babesia microti
occur in Europe and are proven aetiological agents of human

babesiosis (Meer-Scherrer et al., 2004; Hildebrandt et al., 2007;
Gray et al., 2010; Holler et al., 2013). Usually, the course of babesio-
sis caused by B. microti is asymptomatic or mild, but it may occur
as a severe infection in splenectomized patients. Circulation of
B. microti in European natural foci is primarily associated with
small rodents. Microtine rodents and probably shrews are the
most important reservoir hosts (Bown et al., 2008; Silaghi et al.,
2012; Nefedova et al., 2013). Phylogenetic analyses confirmed that
B. microti is a complex species, consisting of genetically diverse
isolates that form different clades based on the analysed genes
(Goethert and Telford, 2003; Nakajima et al., 2009). Within these
clades, rodent isolates are subdivided into the zoonotic“Jena” type
(GenBank accession number EF413181) (Hildebrandt et al., 2007)
and the non-zoonotic “Munich” type (GenBank accession num-
ber AB071177) strains (reviewed in Gray et al., 2010). Different
B. microti strains may circulate in a given natural focus in differ-
ent rodent species at the same time. There are assumptions that in
the circulation of human pathogenic ecotypes, the yellow-necked
mouse (Apodemus flavicollis), which is very frequent in natural
foci of Slovakia, might be predominantly involved (Stanko, 1989,
The main aims of our study were to monitor the infection
prevalence and genetic diversity of Candidatus N. mikurensis and
B. microti in order to elucidate their ecological associations with
rodents, questing I. ricinus, and feeding ticks (I. ricinus and Ixodes
trianguliceps) collected from rodents at four selected sites of Slo-
vakia.

Sample collection
Questing I. ricinus nymphs and adults were collected twice a year
(June and September) during two consecutive years 2011–2012
at four selected sites in Eastern Slovakia. Ticks were collected at
each study site by flagging with a
white corduroy cloth for
one hour to cover various types of forest/shrubland and edge veg-
etation. Immediately after the collection, ticks were identified to
species and sex according to morphological key (Filippova, 1977;
Estrada-Penaˇ et al., 2004) and preserved in
ethanol until the
DNA was extracted.
Trapping of rodents and removal of rodent-fed ticks were
performed during 2011–2013 at four sampling sites in East-
ern Slovakia. Rodents were trapped alive using Swedish bridge
metal traps following the protocol of Stanko (1995). Rodent trap-
pings were carried out using 100–150 live-traps/per site for two
consecutive nights. Small mammals, rodents and insectivores,
were euthanized in a humane manner in accordance with the
laws of the Slovak Republic under the licenses of the Ministry
of Environment of the Slovak Republic No. 297/108/06-3.1 and
No. 6743/2008-2.1. Rodent-fed ticks were removed with sterile
forceps, counted, and identified to life stage and species using pre-
viously published taxonomic keys (Filippova, 1977; Estrada-Penaˇ
et al., 2004) and preserved in
ethanol until DNA extraction. A
maximum of 20 feeding and visibly engorged I. ricinus ticks per
captured rodent and all feeding I. trianguliceps ticks were ana-
lysed. Moreover, spleen and ear biopsies were obtained from each
rodent and rodent foetuses from gravid females during necroscopy

estimated using the study of Pelikán (1966), assuming the preg-

23–24 days.
DNA extraction
Questing ticks and ticks removed from rodents were further
analysed by DNA based methods. Genomic DNA was isolated from
individual ticks by alcaline-hydrolysis according to Guy and Stanek
(1991). DNA from rodent tissues was extracted using a commercial
DNA extraction kit (NucleoSpin Blood kit, NucleoSpin Tissue kit,
Machery Nagel, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s proto-
col. Lysates were stored at
- 2 0 ^ { \circ } C
Molecular detection of pathogens
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of the tick mito-
chondrial cytochrome b gene and 12S rRNA gene of vertebrates was
performed for each sample as a quality control for extracted tick and
tissue DNA, respectively (Black and Roehrdanz, 1998; Derdakova
et al., 2003; Humair et al., 2007).
Only positive samples were further screened for the pres-
ence of Candidatus N. mikurensis by real-time PCR using the
primers NMGroELF, NMGroELR and the NMikGroEL-P2a TaqMan-
Probe labelled with Texas Red, which targeted a 99-bp long
fragment of the groEL gene (Jahfari et al., 2012). This assay was
run on a CFX96 Real-Time PCR System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA,
USA). To further characterize Candidatus N. mikurensis-positive
samples, two molecular loci, 16S rRNA and gltA were amplified
and sequenced. Single PCRs were performed to amplify a 560-bp
fragment of the 16S rRNA gene using the primers IS58-594r and
IS58-62f as previously described (Kawahara et al., 2004) and a
233-bp fragment of the gltA gene with the primers NMikfogltA,
NMikregltA (Jahfari et al., 2012).
For the molecular detection of Babesia spp., PCR amplification of
a 450-bp fragment of the small 18S subunit of ribosomal RNA with
primers BJ1 and BN2 was performed (Casati et al., 2006).

Sequence analysis: 16S rRNA and gltA gene sequences of
Candidatus N. mikurensis
In samples which tested positive for Candidatus N. mikurensis
groEL gene, we further amplified and sequenced two other genetic
loci, 16S rRNA and gltA. Four Candidatus N. mikurensis 16S rRNA
(KJ649314–KJ649316, KJ649323) and six Candidatus N. mikuren-
sis gltA (KJ649317–KJ322) sequences were deposited in GenBank
database (Table 3).
The obtained Candidatus N. mikurensis 16S rRNA sequences
from rodent spleen biopsies, from feeding ticks removed from
rodents, and from I. ricinus ticks from vegetation showed
iden-
tity with the various Candidatus N. mikurensis isolates deposited
in GenBank, e.g. an isolate from an I. persulcatus tick from Rus-
sia (FJ966360), nucleotide sequences from rodents from China
(JQ359052) and Japan (AB196305), that were also identical with
a human isolate from China (JQ359045).
The nucleotide sequences of Candidatus N. mikurensis gltA gene
from rodent spleen biopsies, from ticks feeding on rodents and from
I. ricinus ticks from vegetation showed
homology with the
Candidatus N. mikurensis isolate taken from an I. ricinus tick from
Italy (AY098729).

B. microti in rodent-feeding ticks
A total of 788 feeding ticks were tested, and 37 I. ricinus ticks
tested positive for B. microti (Table 4). B. microti-positive I.
ricinus ticks (32 larvae and 3 nymphs) were collected from A. agrar-
ius and one larva and nymph were removed from A. flavicollis from
the site Botanical garden in Kosiceˇ (Tables 5 and 6).
B. microti in questing I. ricinus ticks
Altogether 1368 questing I. ricinus ticks were tested for the pres-
ence of B. microti by PCR targeting the 18S rRNA gene resulting
in an overall B. microti infection prevalence of
0.16–0.96). DNA of B. microti was found in questing nymphal I. rici-
nus
and questing adult I. ricinus ticks

strain” (GenBank accession number EF413181) in 24 B. microti-
positive samples
KJ649303–KJ649312) and the “non-zoonotic” strain (GenBank
accession number AB071177) in two B. microti isolates

sequences were

Discussion
In the present study, we investigated the prevalence of infection
and diversity of Candidatus N. mikurensis and B. microti in rodents,
in questing and in feeding ticks (I. ricinus and I. trianguliceps) col-
lected from rodents. We conducted a comparative study in two
sites known for the occurrence of I. ricinus only (Botanical garden
Kosice, ˇ Rozhanovce) and two sites at a higher altitude (600–750 m
asl) (Cermel’ ˇ and Hyl’ov) ´ where both tick species (I. ricinus and I.
trianguliceps) occur (Petko et al., 1991). In this study, we did not find
significant differences among the infection prevalence of Candida-
tus N. mikurensis in spleen samples and questing I. ricinus ticks
from different sites. In contrast, we found significant differences
among the prevalence of B. microti in ear and spleen biopsies and
questing I. ricinus ticks from different sites. The highest prevalence
of B. microti in rodent biopsies was observed in urban park Botan-
ical garden that might indicate the presence of suitable reservoir
hosts in urban areas.
The overall prevalence of Candidatus N. mikurensis infection
in rodent spleen biopsies (M. glareolus and Apodemus spp.) in our
study was
. Other authors from Europe reported the rate of
infection in different rodent organs (kidney, liver, skin, and brain)
varies from
up to
(Jahfari et al., 2012; Silaghi et al.,
2012; Burri et al., 2014). Candidatus N. mikurensis was detected
at selected sites where I. trianguliceps ticks were present. None of
the 790 rodent ear biopsies tested positive. In eco-epidemiological
studies of Silaghi et al. (2012), different animal organs were used
as the source of genomic DNA extraction and further detection of
Candidatus N. mikurensis DNA. After experimental infection of rats,
no infection was observed after 15 days in blood, spleen or liver, a
weak infection was detected in the spleen after 30 days, and in all
three organs 60 days after initial infection. This is in accordance
with our results that that spleen and kidneys are the most appro-
priate organs for detection of Candidatus N. mikurensis in rodents.
As confirmed in present study, skin biopsies are not suitable for
molecular identification of Candidatus N. mikurensis.
A recent study conducted by Burri et al. (2014) using xeno-
diagnosis, found that M. glareolus and A. flavicollis are reservoirs
of Candidatus N. mikurensis. Similarly as in our study, the bac-

Conclusion
The results of this study confirmed that in natural foci of Slo-
vakia, rodents are infected with Candidatus N. mikurensis and B.
microti and might act as reservoir hosts of both pathogens by infect-
ing the feeding ticks. Both, questing nymphal and adult I. ricinus and
feeding larval and nymphal I. ricinus ticks as well as feeding larval I.
trianguliceps ticks were found to be infected. To our knowledge, the
presence of Candidatus N. mikurensis in the rodent-feeding larval I.
trianguliceps was demonstrated for the first time in Europe. Molec-
ular evidence of B. microti in rodent foetuses suggests the possibility
of transplacental transmission as an alternative route for the spread
of infection among rodents.
